{"id": "14:38/q02", "question": "Does 'Our Lord' differ from 'my Lord' in this prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular and plural address carry distinct grounds or scope for the appeal.", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q02/p1", "position": "The two forms have no apparent difference here.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan explicitly sees no apparent distinction between addressing God as my Lord and our Lord."}, {"id": "14:38/q02/p2", "position": "The plural address is apt because it encompasses a wider circle of hidden matters.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the plural reaches all hidden things in God's kingdom and dominion, as the following clause explains, and objects to Abu Hayyan's denial of a difference."}, {"id": "14:38/q02/p3", "position": "Rabbi invokes a favor personally experienced; Rabbana invokes one witnessed by all God's creatures.", "reasons": "Islahi makes the difference depend on the reach of the favor cited as grounds for a plea."}]}
{"id": "14:38/q03", "question": "What are the things Abraham says God knows they hide and disclose?", "turns_on": "Whether the words cover all affairs or identify a particular inward and outward pair, and which episode or inward state supplies that pair.", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q03/p1", "position": "All their private and public affairs, including needs, states, and desires.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari includes the family's motives and sincere worship (14:35); al-Kashshaf, al-Baydawi, al-Biqa'i, and al-Alusi include needs and interests; Ibn Atiyya includes guidance and care for children. Abu Hayyan explicitly prefers the general scope only indirectly through his reading of the following expansion; al-Alusi explicitly prefers the general reading and says it includes states unknown even to Abraham. Al-Tabataba'i calls the meaning plain."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p2", "position": "His concealed intent is God's approval and obedient, sincere worship by his descendants.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari links the motive to the prayer for the town in 14:35; Ibn Kathir transmits Ibn Jarir's explanation that the prayer for its people seeks God's pleasure alone."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p3", "position": "He hid distress or grief over Ishmael in the barren valley and openly said he had settled his descendants there.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies Ishmael's foreign place without water or livelihood and identifies the valley as Mecca; a report in al-Jishumi likewise contrasts hidden grief with the spoken statement."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p4", "position": "He concealed grief over Ishmael and made his apprehension public.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports this wording from Ibn Abbas."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p5", "position": "His longing or affection for Ishmael and Hajar is among what is hidden and revealed.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, and al-Qurtubi attribute this to Ibn Abbas and Muqatil after the family was settled in the barren valley; they do not assign the feeling exclusively to either side of the pair."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p6", "position": "He hid grief at separation and openly wept, prayed, or relied on God.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari's Ibn Abbas report places their grief after Abraham left Hajar and Ishmael in Mecca. Al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan, and al-Alusi report public crying and prayer; al-Baydawi adds reliance on God."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p7", "position": "He hid sorrow at parting and publicly entrusted Hajar and Ishmael to God in their farewell exchange.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan, and al-Alusi recount Hajar asking whom he left them to; Abraham answered God. In the fuller forms she asks whether God commanded it and accepts that they need not fear or will be safe."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p8", "position": "He concealed anguish at leaving Ishmael but openly displayed love for him.", "reasons": "Abu Salih transmits this from Ibn Abbas in Ibn al-Jawzi; the commentators place the speech when Ishmael had been settled in the sanctuary and Abraham was about to leave."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p9", "position": "He hid love for Ishmael and Hajar but outwardly showed harshness or estrangement toward them.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports hidden love and outward harshness from Ibn Abbas; al-Alusi transmits from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i through Ibn Abi Hatim that he openly showed Sarah estrangement. The formulations of the outward display differ."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p10", "position": "Their hidden and public matter is monotheism.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports this identification from al-Asamm."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p11", "position": "The hidden is love of God and the declared is remembrance of Him.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami reports al-Khawwas's inward reading."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p12", "position": "The hidden is spiritual states and the manifest is proper devotional conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami reports Ibn Ata's inward reading."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p13", "position": "The hidden is companionship with God and the declared is ecstatic love.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami reports al-Husayn's inward reading."}, {"id": "14:38/q03/p14", "position": "The hidden is potential within us and the declared is perfections brought into actuality.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani pairs these with God's knowledge of the earth of capacity and heaven of spirit."}]}
{"id": "14:38/q04", "question": "How does ma function in 'what we hide and what we disclose'?", "turns_on": "Whether ma names things concealed and disclosed or turns the verbs into verbal nouns.", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q04/p1", "position": "Ma is a relative pronoun referring to concealed and disclosed things.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the reported specific explanations construe ma as relative, with an omitted antecedent."}, {"id": "14:38/q04/p2", "position": "Ma can be a verbal noun, yielding 'our secrecy as our publicity.'", "reasons": "Al-Alusi gives this as another grammatical analysis."}]}
{"id": "14:38/q05", "question": "Why is the hidden mentioned before the public?", "turns_on": "Whether the order emphasizes God's reach into secrecy or follows the order from secrecy to disclosure.", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q05/p1", "position": "Hiddenness comes first to stress that God's knowledge reaches it as fully as the manifest.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the less visible side receives priority to establish equal divine knowledge."}, {"id": "14:38/q05/p2", "position": "Secrecy precedes public disclosure, so knowledge of it is mentioned first.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi also offers this sequence of events as an explanation."}]}
{"id": "14:38/q06", "question": "Why voice needs to God when He already knows them?", "turns_on": "Whether the stated knowledge chiefly entrusts unspoken needs to God or attests the petitioner's motive.", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q06/p1", "position": "Prayer entrusts needs and unspoken desires to the One who knows them best, while displaying servitude, humility, dependence, and hope for mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf and al-Baydawi say God knows needs better and is more merciful; al-Kashshaf cites a petitioner who speaks from need, not to remind a forgetful patron. Al-Razi says Abraham cannot know future outcomes but God knows interests and harms. Ibn Atiyya says his compact plea entrusts guidance and care for his children to God. Al-Bursevi and al-Alusi say articulation manifests need and eagerness for gifts; al-Alusi cites al-Suhrawardi's verse that God knows a complaint before it is spoken. Al-Biqa'i says prayer supplies no information. Study Quran adds 3:29 and says supplication hastens response. Islah

{"id": "14:38/q08", "question": "How extensive is God's knowledge in the final clause?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q08/p1", "position": "It includes every thing and every hidden or public state in full detail, without any temporal or creaturely limit.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Tha'labi, al-Qushayri, al-Tabrisi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi, al-Biqa'i, al-Tabataba'i, and Asad state the universal scope. Ibn Atiyya stresses fully detailed knowledge. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi ground it in God's essential knowledge, equally related to every object; al-Bursevi adds that past, present, and future do not apply to Him and contrasts acquired human or angelic knowledge. {"id": "14:38/q09", "question": "Why phrase universal knowledge as 'nothing is hidden'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q09/p1", "position": "The negative wording emphatically excludes every trace of obscurity from divine knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi contrasts God's knowledge with creaturely knowledge, where obscurity exists. {"id": "14:38/q10", "question": "What does min contribute to 'nothing'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q10/p1", "position": "It makes the negation exhaustive: not a single thing is hidden.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, and al-Bursevi expressly give this force; al-Biqa'i also notes the generic 'anything' in the emphatic universal wording."}]}
{"id": "14:38/q11", "question": "What does 'in earth and in heaven' grammatically modify?", "turns_on": "Whether the location qualifies the thing or the act of being hidden.", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q11/p1", "position": "It describes the thing: no thing located in earth or heaven is hidden.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevi allows this attachment. {"id": "14:38/q12", "question": "What do 'earth' and 'heaven' encompass here?", "turns_on": "Whether the two realms are spatial, directional, perceptual, or inward images.", "positions": [{"id": "14:38/q12/p1", "position": "Earth and all the heavens are the literal lower and upper realms.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the singular al-sama' includes all heavens and that earth is the nearer realm."}, {"id": "14:38/q12/p2", "position": "They may mean the lower and upper directions.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi offers this alternative to the literal account of earth and heaven."}, {"id": "14:38/q12/p3", "position": "Earth may mean what humans perceive and heaven what is hidden from human perception.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i proposes this perceptual distinction."}, {"id": "14:38/q12/p4", "position": "Earth is capacity and heaven is spirit.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani uses this inward correspondence for God's knowledge of potential and actual perfections."}]}

{"id": "14:40/q01", "question": "Why does the prayer use 'my Lord' and 'our Lord,' and repeat the address?", "turns_on": "The notes explain different functions of the address and repetition, without setting them against each other.", "positions": [{"id": "14:40/q01/p1", "position": "The singular addresses Abraham's own experience or precedence; the plural voices a request shared with his descendants or a favor witnessed by all.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes requests specific to Abraham's precedence and imamate from shared requests. {"id": "14:40/q02", "question": "What does asking God to make Abraham establish prayer imply about human action?", "turns_on": "How God's making the act relates to the servant's own undertaking: creation, enabling grace, or divine permission alongside human action.", "positions": [{"id": "14:40/q02/p1", "position": "God creates or alone brings about the commanded act of prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī argues that making prayer for Abraham is creating prayer for him and hence human acts are created. {"id": "14:40/q03", "question": "What does it mean to be a maintainer of prayer here?", "turns_on": "Whether prayer names sustained ritual observance, broader steadfast devotion, or an inward state.", "positions": [{"id": "14:40/q03/p1", "position": "To perform prayer soundly and persist in its regular observance.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī identifies the prayer God obligated and worshipful obedience. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say the already praying Abraham sought continuation; Ibn ʿĀshūr reads ajʿalnī as bringing him into that future state. Wāḥidī, Asad, and Study Quran also describe constancy or persistent actual practice."}, {"id": "14:40/q03/p2", "position": "To remain firm in religion or wholly devoted to God.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī glosses it as steadfastness in Islam and its rulings. Bursawī calls prayer the believer's miʿrāj and reads its establishment as continuous ascent in and through God."}]}
{"id": "14:40/q04", "question": "Why say 'one who establishes prayer' rather than use a verb?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:40/q04/p1", "position": "The adjectival or participial form asks for an enduring state of prayer keeping.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says the adjective is more enduring and emphatic than asking to perform an action, with a link to 17:29. {"id": "14:40/q12", "question": "How is Warsh's lengthening in 'accept my prayer' analyzed?", "turns_on": "Whether incidental opening or orthographic loss affects the length, or the underlying form governs it.", "positions": [{"id": "14:40/q12/p1", "position": "Treat it by Warsh's usual lengthening pattern according to the underlying form.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī groups wa-taqabbal duʿāʾ with millat ābāʾī Ibrāhīm and fa-lam yazidhum duʿāʾī illā, disregarding incidental opening or written deletion; he says this is his analogy learned in performance for Abraham's duʿāʾ."}, {"id": "14:40/q12/p2", "position": "In the discussed incidental case, shortening is more likely, though lengthening is possible under the general rule.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reasons that both hamzat al-waṣl and initial position are incidental, so they should not govern length."}]}
{"id": "14:40/q13", "question": "What reports describe the effect of Abraham's prayer on his descendants?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different outcomes of the prayer rather than competing counts or persons.", "positions": [{"id": "14:40/q13/p1", "position": "God answered Abraham's requests, including descendants' prayer, avoidance of idols, and other blessings.", "reasons": "Kashshāf reports Mujāhid: no descendant worshipped an idol afterward; the land became safe and fruitful; Abraham became an imam; some descendants established prayer; God taught him the rites and accepted his repentance."}, {"id": "14:40/q13/p2", "position": "Some descendants remain on the natural faith, worshipping God until the Hour.", "reasons": "Nasafī reports Ibn ʿAbbās; Durr reports Ibn Jurayj, who explicitly says they worship God."}]}
